summary: Describes approaches and shows signaling and media flow examples for session mobility, where a call is moved from one device to another using SIP. Service discovery is essential. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: You start a video call on your phone and then pass it to your laptop without hanging up. This explains how.

subtitle: Move an active call from one device to another without hanging up.

tldr.problem: A user in an active audio or video call needs to switch devices mid-session, such as moving from a mobile phone to a desktop with a larger screen, or losing battery and needing to continue on another device.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile node (controlling device) uses SIP signaling to either manage the transfer itself using third-party call control, or to have a local device take over the call by referring the remote participant to connect directly to the new device.
tldr.outcome: The session continues without interruption on the new device, though seamlessly splitting a session across multiple devices requires more complex coordination.

facts.label: Key transfer modes
facts.value: Mobile Node Control (MNC) and Session Handoff (SH)

facts.label: SIP methods used
facts.value: INVITE, REFER, OPTIONS, ACK, BYE, NOTIFY

today: RFC 5631 is an Informational RFC describing a framework for session mobility using SIP. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and outlines approaches that can be implemented by SIP systems that need to support mid-call device switching.

sections.title: Session Mobility Overview
sections.content:
Session mobility is the ability to transfer an active multimedia session from one device to another during the call. This is useful for mobile users who want to take advantage of nearby devices with better capabilities, such as moving a video call from a mobile phone to a desktop with a larger screen.

The framework requires two capabilities: device discovery (to locate available devices and learn their capabilities) and session transfer mechanisms (to move the call itself). This RFC describes approaches using SIP, the Session Initiation Protocol, along with device discovery using the Service Location Protocol (SLP). The framework distinguishes between basic devices (standard SIP endpoints) and enhanced devices (with session mobility capabilities).
sections.plainLanguage: Your devices talk to each other so they know what they can do. When you ask your phone to move a call to your laptop, the call smoothly switches.

sections.title: Two Transfer Modes: Control and Handoff
sections.content:
The RFC defines two modes for transferring sessions. In Mobile Node Control (MNC) mode, the mobile node (your device) stays in the middle, acting as a third-party call controller. It establishes separate sessions with both the local device (where the media is moving to) and the remote participant, then updates both sessions' media parameters so the local device and remote participant send media directly to each other. The MN remains active to maintain these sessions.

In Session Handoff (SH) mode, the mobile node uses the SIP REFER method to ask the local device to invite the remote participant to a new session, effectively handing off complete control. The SIP Replaces header tells the remote participant to replace its session with the MN with the new session from the local device. This is useful when the MN needs to disconnect (low battery, losing connectivity) and wants the call to continue independently.
sections.plainLanguage: MNC mode: You stay on the call, connecting your laptop to your friend so they talk directly. SH mode: You give your laptop the ability to talk to your friend instead, and you step away.

sections.title: Device Discovery and Capabilities
sections.content:
Before a session can be transferred, the mobile node must discover what devices are available and what they can do. The RFC uses the Service Location Protocol (SLP), which allows devices in a network to register their services and capabilities as attribute-value pairs. A device might advertise that it supports audio and video at a certain resolution and bandwidth.

Devices register themselves to an SLP Directory Agent (DA), which maintains a list of available services. The mobile node queries the DA for available sip-device services in its location, receives a list of device URIs, and queries each one for details like supported codecs and display resolution. In the simplest case, devices can also be pre-configured with known media server addresses instead of using dynamic discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone asks the network, 'What devices are here and what can they do?' A helpful service answers with a list of your nearby laptop, TV, and wireless speaker, along with what each can handle.

sections.title: Splitting and Retrieving Sessions
sections.content:
A user can transfer just one part of a session (such as video) while keeping another part (such as audio) on the original device. For example, the MN might transfer video to a large screen while continuing audio on a headset. The MN constructs media parameters for the remote participant that combine some parameters from the new device and others from itself.

Sessions can also be retrieved. If a user transfers a call to a local device and then walks away, they can initiate a retrieval to bring the session back to their mobile device. In SH mode, this involves a nested REFER: the MN sends a REFER asking the local device to send it a REFER back, with instructions to connect to the remote participant and replace the current session.

The RFC also handles multiple-device systems: a device can discover nearby devices and group them as a 'virtual device' that presents unified capabilities, allowing a session to be split smoothly across them.
sections.plainLanguage: You can move just the video to your big screen while keeping audio on your phone. Later, you can grab everything back to your phone with a gesture.

sections.title: Security and Codec Compatibility
sections.content:
Session handoff uses the Replaces header, which must be verified to prevent unauthorized users from hijacking calls. The RFC uses S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) to sign the REFER request, so the remote participant knows the handoff is authorized by the original session participant.

Device capability differences must be resolved before transfer. If the new device doesn't support the same codec as the current session, the MN can invoke a transcoder service to translate between media streams. The MN queries both the remote participant and the local device for their supported codecs using the SIP OPTIONS method and SLP attributes. If a common codec exists, it is negotiated. If not, a transcoding service is discovered and enlisted to bridge the incompatibility.

Display resolution and bandwidth differences are addressed similarly: the MN may downgrade video to lower resolution for bandwidth-constrained devices.
sections.plainLanguage: Your laptop and phone speak different languages? A helper translator converts between them. The system signs the handoff so nobody can fake it.
